clinical: Acute pancreatitis
Digestive enzymes switch on inside the acinar cells instead of in the gut, so the gland starts digesting itself and becomes inflamed. Gallstones and heavy alcohol use are the most common causes.
Chronic pancreatitis
Long-standing damage destroys acinar cells and replaces them with scar tissue, so too few digestive enzymes reach the gut and fat is poorly absorbed (greasy, pale stools).
Pancreatic cancer
Most pancreatic cancers (ductal adenocarcinoma) start in the lining of the ducts rather than in the acini.
Cystic fibrosis
A faulty chloride channel (CFTR) in duct cells makes the secretions thick and sticky, blocking the ducts so enzymes cannot reach the gut.
Type 1 diabetes
The immune system destroys the beta cells, so little or no insulin is made and blood glucose rises.
Insulinoma
A rare tumour of beta cells that releases too much insulin, causing dangerously low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia).
Scarring in chronic pancreatitis
As acini are lost in chronic pancreatitis, the septa thicken with scar tissue, so the gland becomes firm and shrunken.
